zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

headline: Slow Monday, stacked Thursday: Norfolk yellowfin save a shaky week
subhead: Poor Man's went dead flat early, but the warm edge held east of Norfolk and turned the back half of the week into real fishing.
body_markdown:
Give this week a C-minus through Wednesday and a solid B by Saturday. That's the honest grade. We ran four different boats to three different canyons this week trying to find where the warm water actually sat, and for the first three days we were chasing our tail. Monday and Tuesday at Poor Man's were about as flat as canyon fishing gets — clean blue water, no real color change, no birds working, and a chunk line that just sat there untouched for four hours before we pulled the anchor and ran. That's the kind of day that makes you second-guess the whole trip, but it's also exactly why I don't commit one boat to one canyon and stay put all week. You've got to be willing to move.

Wednesday we made the call to run south to Norfolk instead of doubling down on Poor Man's, and that's where the week turned. The warm-water edge that's been sitting east of the canyons all month held its position, and where that blue water pushed up against the cooler green stuff along the drop, we found bait balled up tight and yellowfin working underneath it. We got bit almost as soon as the chunk hit the water — butterflied bunker on 60-pound fluoro leader, 6/0 circle hooks, fished with just enough weight to get down through the top twenty feet where the fish were holding. That bite ran steady through the afternoon in 250 to 300 feet of water right on the edge, fish mostly in the 25 to 45 pound class with a couple pushing bigger. Not a stacked-boat, gaff-every-five-minutes bite, but a real, consistent pick that kept rods bent most of the day.

Thursday and Friday we stayed in that same general area off Norfolk and found mahi scattered around anything holding structure — a mat of sargassum, a few pieces of debris, even a stray lobster trap buoy line. Small stuff mostly, schoolies in the 3 to 8 pound range, but they came fast on bucktail-tipped Sabiki rigs once we found the first pod and worked it slow with chunks tossed to hold them up. If you find one mahi under a weed line, don't run off it — circle back, toss a few pieces of butterfished bait, and let the school show itself. We also had two white marlin flags Friday afternoon working a dredge and naked ballyhoo combo behind the spreader bars, raised one and got him to eat a hookless teaser but never converted it to a pitch bait in time. That's canyon marlin fishing in a nutshell some days — you get the shot, you don't always get the fish.

Saturday we pushed north to Spencer to see if the pattern was holding up the whole range, and it was mixed. Morning troll produced two bigeye mixed in with the yellowfin on the same spread — green-and-yellow Ilanders and small horse ballyhoo pulled at 6 to 7 knots along the 100-fathom break — but the afternoon chunk went quiet once the current slacked off. Bigeye showing up mixed into a yellowfin bite this time of year usually means the thermocline's still healthy and there's enough depth of warm water for those fish to sit deeper during the day and come up on the chunk in low light. We didn't stick around long enough Saturday to test that theory into the evening, which in hindsight might have been the move.

We never got to Lindenkohl this week — sea state kept building out of the southeast by Friday and it wasn't worth the extra run when Norfolk and Spencer were both producing. That's the tradeoff running four canyons out of Cape May and Ocean City always presents: you can't fish them all in one week, so you commit based on where the water's telling you to go, and this week that water was clearly sitting east of Norfolk and holding along the Spencer break.

On the wahoo front — nothing solid yet, but there's chatter building. A few boats working the high-speed troll with cedar plugs and small Ilanders behind planers off the deeper water past Norfolk have had a couple of gray ghosts show interest without committing, slashing bait off the line without eating hooks clean. That's usually the first sign before a real wahoo run gets going, and if this warm pool holds its position through the next week like it has the last ten days, I'd expect that bite to firm up. Worth running a dedicated wahoo spread — one or two lines with wire leader and a planer down deep — even while you're primarily fishing the tuna troll, because right now you genuinely don't know which fish is going to show up first.

Looking ahead, the call for next week is simple: stick with the warm edge as long as it holds east of the canyons. If it slides west or starts breaking apart, that yellowfin bite at Norfolk could get patchy fast, and I'd shift effort back toward Spencer where the bottom structure tends to hold fish even when the surface temperature break gets messy. Moon's past new and building toward the quarter, which should mean better current flow on the edges over the next few days — that's usually when the chunk bite tightens up and stays consistent through a full tide cycle instead of turning on and off. If you've got one shot this week, I'd take the early run to Norfolk, get bait in the water by first light, and be ready to move if the color change isn't where it was Wednesday. It moves. You've got to move with it.
